all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: integration
concepts.definition: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

defining_facts.text: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

concepts.name: interaction design
concepts.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

defining_facts.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: prototype
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.
Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

concepts.name: iteration
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin.

The design-prototype-evaluate loop and each of its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise the overall turnaround time will increase significantly.

concepts.name: requirement gathering
concepts.definition: The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

defining_facts.text: The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

concepts.name: design-prototype-evaluate cycle
concepts.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development has iterations between its design, prototyping, and early evaluation stages, and it also has an iteration to the requirement gathering stage.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.
In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the term design refers only to interface and interaction design, not code design.

A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.

The interface design part of interactive system development uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle comprising design, prototyping, and quick evaluation of the prototype; design may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, quick evaluation may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the cycle is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.

Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable; usability testing or an empirical study is therefore needed to estimate usability, although usability was expected because the design-prototype-evaluate cycle was followed.

In the traditional interactive system development lifecycle, the requirement gathering stage may span months; the design-prototype-evaluate stage can take months, although each cycle may take one or two days and, considering repeated cycles and other activities, may take from a couple of weeks to a month; code design may take months or at least a couple of weeks; code testing may take weeks; and an empirical study may take weeks.

concepts.name: design
concepts.definition: In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

defining_facts.text: In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

concepts.name: code design
concepts.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.

defining_facts.text: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

concepts.name: code testing
concepts.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

defining_facts.text: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.

The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.
Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.
The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.

An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.

concepts.name: requirement
concepts.definition: A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.

defining_facts.text: A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.

concepts.name: interface design
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: interactive system development lifecycle
concepts.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

defining_facts.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

concepts.name: testing
concepts.definition: A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

defining_facts.text: A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

concepts.name: functional requirement
concepts.definition: Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements.

defining_facts.text: Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements.
Functional requirements are the system features and abilities to carry out tasks, expressed as functions treated as black boxes that produce an output from an input once implemented.
The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.

Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier.

A functional requirement (FR) is a formally specifiable requirement that is easy to convert into code because it specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input, a well-defined output, and an optional description of its purpose.

Usability requirements, which are non-functional requirements (NFRs), can be converted into functional requirements (FRs) and added to the already obtained set of functional requirements, so that usability requirements are directly incorporated into the system through code and support code design.

A software requirements specification (SRS) is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements.

The output of contextual inquiry is a group-wise organization of the notes taken during observation, and it can be used as design guidelines to ensure usability that cannot be immediately converted to code or, for some of them if not all, converted into functional requirements (FRs) that can be directly implemented as code.

In the calendar app for college students example, the functional requirement R1 views takes a date as input and generates a specific view such as timetable, submission deadlines, or meeting list, with subrequirements R1.1 timetable view (date input, day timetable output), R1.2 deadline view (date input, submission deadlines output), and R1.3 meeting schedule (date input, list of meetings scheduled on the day output).

concepts.name: non-functional requirement
concepts.definition: Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements.

defining_facts.text: Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements.
Non-functional requirements are system characteristics that cannot be expressed as functions and are typically related to quality attributes of software.
Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.
Categories of non-functional requirements include performance-related requirements, operating constraints, economic considerations, lifecycle requirements, and interface issues.

concepts.name: usability requirement
concepts.definition: Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.

defining_facts.text: Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.

concepts.name: design guideline
concepts.definition: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested to determine whether it will work.

defining_facts.text: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested to determine whether it will work.

concepts.name: software requirements specification
concepts.definition: A software requirements specification (SRS) is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements.

defining_facts.text: A software requirements specification (SRS) is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements.

In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

concepts.name: design language
concepts.definition: Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.

defining_facts.text: Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.

A design language is a specification of design, and there can be different languages for specifying a design; the language used to specify interface design is generally different from the language used to specify code design.

concepts.name: cognitive walkthrough
concepts.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

defining_facts.text: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.

A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.

Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.

concepts.name: heuristic evaluation
concepts.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

defining_facts.text: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

Nielsen's 10 heuristics can be used to identify usability problems at an early stage of design on the basis of simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional in heuristic evaluation, unlike the cognitive walkthrough method, where a vertical prototype is mandatory.
Heuristic evaluation requires a team of at least three to five evaluators, who can be members of design teams or other skilled or expert designers not necessarily involved in the design team.

In heuristic evaluation, each evaluator is given the prototype and the checklist of heuristics, evaluates the prototype against each heuristic, reports whether each heuristic is followed or violated and, if violated, gives reasons, and the evaluators' reports are combined and compiled to identify the violated heuristics and major issues.
